92.title: Bernadette at Lourdes (1858)
92.hook: a sick, poor, fourteen-year-old sees a lady in a grotto and digs where a spring appears
92.carry: she was only asked to tell
92.howItsDone: Catholics keep the feast of Our Lady of Lourdes on February 11, also the World Day of the Sick; millions of pilgrims visit the grotto each year, many of them ill, to pray, join the candlelight processions and bathe in the spring water.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Thomas More, who refused an oath in silence. Your line was the king's good servant, God's first. Did you keep your quiet promise? This week, the modern saints. Day ninety-two.

February 1858, a small town in the foothills of the Pyrenees. It's cold. A girl of fourteen goes out with her sister and a friend to gather firewood and bones to sell. She's small for her age, she has asthma, and she can't read. Her family is so poor they're living in one damp room that used to be the town jail. The other two cross a stream. She hesitates at the cold water, near a rocky hollow in the cliff called Massabielle. Then she hears a sound like wind, looks up, and sees, in the grotto, a young lady dressed in white, smiling at her. Today: Bernadette at Lourdes.
screen: `FEBRUARY 1858.` → `A GIRL GATHERING WOOD.` → `A LADY IN THE GROTTO.`

segments.voice: Her name was Bernadette Soubirous. Over that spring and summer she said the lady appeared to her eighteen times. Crowds began to follow her to the grotto. They saw nothing but a girl kneeling, her face changed. Then, on one of the visits, Bernadette said the lady told her to drink from the spring and wash in it. There was no spring. So she scratched at the muddy ground with her hands, and tried to drink the dirty water, and smeared her face. People thought she'd lost her mind. But over the next days, water began to flow from that spot, and it still flows. Weeks later, she asked the lady her name. The answer came in the local dialect, in words Bernadette didn't understand: I am the Immaculate Conception. She repeated them all the way to the parish priest so she wouldn't forget. He went pale. That title for Mary had been defined by the Pope only four years before, and he doubted this girl had ever heard it. The police questioned her, and so did the clergy. She never changed her story, and she never tried to convince anyone. She said, in effect, that her job was to tell, not to make people believe. She later became a nun, suffered long illness, and died at thirty-five. Catholics call apparitions like this private revelation: the Church approved Lourdes, but no Catholic is required to believe it. Millions go anyway, many of them sick, to bathe in the water and to pray.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hold someone who is ill. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one person who is sick right now, in body or in mind. See their face. Picture them the way pilgrims picture the ones they carry to Lourdes: not fixed, just held, just brought. If you pray, you can pray for them now, maybe with a Hail Mary. If you don't, simply hold them in your attention and wish them well. The bell holds the time.
Massabielle. The grotto where a poor, sick girl saw a lady in white, and dug for a hidden spring.
Your line: she was only asked to tell. Today, say one true thing plainly, and let it go. You don't have to win the argument. Day ninety-two.

93.title: Thérèse of Lisieux (1873–1897)
93.hook: she died at 24 in an obscure convent and became one of the most loved saints
93.howItsDone: Catholics keep the feast of St. Thérèse on October 1, read her autobiography Story of a Soul, and many ask her prayers in novenas; she is a patron of the missions, though she never left her convent.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bernadette at Lourdes, who dug at Massabielle where the spring appeared. Your line was she was only asked to tell. Did you say one true thing and let it go? Day ninety-three.

A girl of fourteen is in Rome with her father and a group of pilgrims, waiting in line to meet the Pope. They've all been told firmly: do not speak to the Holy Father. When her turn comes, she kneels, puts her hands on his knees, and asks him anyway. She wants to enter a convent now, at fifteen, not years later. He tells her, gently, that she will enter if God wills it. She has to be carried away by the guards. A few months later she's inside the Carmelite convent in the small French town of Lisieux. She'll never leave it. She'll die there at twenty-four, and almost nobody outside will have heard of her. Today, Thérèse.
screen: `A GIRL KNEELS BEFORE THE POPE.` → `A CONVENT AT FIFTEEN.` → `DEAD AT TWENTY-FOUR.`

segments.voice: Thérèse Martin grew up the youngest of five sisters in a devout family. Her mother died when she was four, and she was a sensitive, tearful child. In the convent she read about the great saints, the martyrs and mystics, and felt tiny beside them. They were mountains. She was a grain of sand. So she went looking for a shortcut. She wrote that in her time, the rich had lifts to save them climbing stairs, and she wanted a lift to God, because she was too small to climb the rough stairway of perfection. She found it in a line of scripture. In the Douay-Rheims: "Whosoever is a little one, let him come to me." The lift, she decided, was the arms of Jesus. She didn't have to become big. She had to stay little and let herself be carried. That's the little way. In practice it looked ordinary. She smiled at a sister who grated on her nerves, so sweetly that the sister thought she was her favorite. When another nun splashed her with dirty water in the laundry, she took it without complaint. Small things, done with great love. In her last illness, dying of tuberculosis, she also went through a deep darkness, when heaven felt closed to her, and she kept going anyway. Her notebooks became a book, Story of a Soul, published a year after she died. It spread around the world. She was canonized in 1925, and in 1997 she was named a Doctor of the Church, one of only a handful of women.
screen: `TOO SMALL FOR THE GREAT SAINTS.` · `A LIFT INSTEAD OF STAIRS.` · `SMALL THINGS, GREAT LOVE.` · `DARKNESS, AND SHE KEPT GOING.` · then, large: `WHOSOEVER IS A LITTLE ONE, LET HIM COME TO ME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pick one small thing to do with great love. Settle, and breathe. Look ahead at your day. Find the smallest, most forgettable task in it: washing a cup, answering a message, holding a door, listening to someone repeat a story. Choose one. Now picture doing it slowly and warmly, as if it mattered, because Thérèse would say it does. If you pray, you can offer it to God before you do it. The bell holds the time.
Little Flower. Thérèse of Lisieux's own nickname, who found a small, hidden way to holiness anyone could walk.
Your line: the little way. Today, do the small thing you picked, with more love than it seems to need, and tell no one. Day ninety-three.

94.title: Maximilian Kolbe (1894–1941)
94.hook: in Auschwitz a Franciscan priest offers to die in place of a father of a family
94.howItsDone: Catholics keep St. Maximilian Kolbe's feast on August 14, the day he died; he is honored as a patron of prisoners and families, and pilgrims pray at the cell in Auschwitz's Block 11 where he died.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Thérèse of Lisieux, the Little Flower, and her little way. Your line was the little way. What small thing did you do with great love? Today's story is heavy. Go gently. Day ninety-four.

Before the war, he was a busy man. A Polish Franciscan friar with round glasses and a head full of plans. He founded a friary near Warsaw that kept growing, ran printing presses, put out magazines, even started a radio station. He traveled to Japan and set up a friary there too. Then, in 1939, Germany invaded Poland. The friary sheltered refugees, Jews among them. In 1941 he was arrested, and that May he was sent to Auschwitz, where he became a number, 16670. Today: Maximilian Kolbe.

First, where we are. Auschwitz was the largest of the Nazi death camps. More than a million people were murdered there, and the great majority were Jews, killed because they were Jews. Poles, Roma, Soviet prisoners and others died there too. Kolbe was one prisoner among very many, and his story sits inside that much larger grief. Here is what happened. In the summer of 1941, a man escaped from Kolbe's block. As punishment, the camp's deputy commander lined the prisoners up and picked ten men to die by starvation in an underground cell. One of them, a Polish sergeant named Franciszek Gajowniczek, cried out for his wife and his children. Then Kolbe stepped out of the line. He said he was a Catholic priest, and he asked to take that man's place. Nobody knows exactly why the officer agreed, but he did. In the starvation cell, survivors said later, Kolbe led the men in prayers and hymns, and the cell was strangely calm. After two weeks, four were still alive, Kolbe among them. On the fourteenth of August, 1941, they were killed with an injection. Gajowniczek survived the war. He lived into his nineties, and he was in Saint Peter's Square in 1982 when Pope John Paul the Second declared Kolbe a saint and a martyr of charity. Catholics hear in this the words of Jesus in the Douay-Rheims: "Greater love than this no man hath, that a man lay down his life for his friends." Kolbe hadn't known the man.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: remember those who died in the camps. Settle, and breathe slowly. This isn't for feeling anything in particular. It's for remembering. Think of the millions murdered in the Holocaust, most of them Jews, whole families, whole towns. Then think of one: a child, a grandmother, a name you may have read. Hold that one person for a while. If you pray, you can pray for the dead. If you don't, keep a silence for them. The bell holds the time.
Maximilian Kolbe. A Franciscan priest who, in Auschwitz, gave his life in place of a stranger with a family. Today's word.
Your line: he stepped forward. Today, when something needs doing and everyone is waiting for someone else, be the one who steps forward, even in a small way. Day ninety-four.

95.title: Teresa of Kolkata (1910–1997)
95.hook: a teacher leaves her convent to care for the dying poor, and writes later of long spiritual darkness
95.tomorrow: Camp 2 close: the cloud of witnesses (Hebrews 12:1)
95.howItsDone: Catholics keep the feast of St. Teresa of Calcutta on September 5, the day she died; the Missionaries of Charity continue her work in homes for the dying, the sick and the abandoned around the world, and volunteers often serve alongside them.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Maximilian Kolbe, who died in a stranger's place in Auschwitz. Your line was he stepped forward. Where did you step forward, even a little? Day ninety-five.

September 1946. A nun in her thirties is on a crowded, overnight train from Calcutta up into the hills of Darjeeling, heading for a retreat. For nearly twenty years she's taught geography and history to girls at a convent school, behind walls, in a city full of people sleeping and dying on the pavements outside. Somewhere on that train, she said later, she heard a call inside her call: leave the convent, and go to live with the poorest of the poor. She was born in Skopje, as Anjezë Bojaxhiu. When she became a nun she took her name from a saint you met two days ago, Thérèse of Lisieux. Today: Teresa of Kolkata.
screen: `A TRAIN TO DARJEELING, 1946.` → `A CALL INSIDE HER CALL.` → `NAMED FOR THÉRÈSE.`

segments.voice: It took her two years to get permission. In 1948 she put on a cheap white sari with blue borders, took some basic nursing training, and walked into the slums with almost nothing. A few of her former students joined her. In 1950 the Church approved her new order, the Missionaries of Charity. Soon after, she opened a home for the dying in an old building beside the Kali temple in Kalighat, where people found in the street could die washed, fed, and held, whatever their religion. She called it Nirmal Hriday, pure heart. The order spread to cities all over the world. In 1979 she received the Nobel Peace Prize. Here's the part few people knew until after she died in 1997. Her letters, published in 2007, showed that for close to fifty years, from around the time she started this work, she felt God's absence. She wrote of darkness and emptiness, and that she no longer felt the presence she'd felt on that train. She kept going anyway, every day, on the floor with the sick. She had critics too, over the medical care in her homes and over some of her funding, and people still argue about that. In 2016 Pope Francis declared her a saint. Her way was close to her namesake's. She is often quoted as saying most of us can't do great things, only small things with great love. Catholics see in her the words of Jesus, in the Douay-Rheims: "as long as you did it to one of these my least brethren, you did it to me."

segments.voice: Here's the practice: see the person in front of you. Settle, and breathe. Think of the next person you'll actually be face to face with today. A coworker. A cashier. Someone at home. Picture their face, and try to see them as she tried to see the dying on the pavement: not a task, not a problem, a person. Notice one thing about them you usually miss. If you pray, you can pray for them by name. The bell holds the time.
Nirmal Hriday. Bengali for pure heart, the home where Teresa of Kolkata let the dying be washed, fed, and held.
Your line: small things with great love. Today, when you meet that person, really look at them, and do one small thing for them well. Day ninety-five.

96.title: Camp 2 close: the cloud of witnesses (Hebrews 12:1)
96.hook: the saints aren't statues but a crowd cheering you on
96.carry: so great a cloud of witnesses
96.tomorrow: First Mass, or first in years
96.howItsDone: Catholics profess the communion of saints in the Apostles' Creed, pray for the dead especially in November and on All Souls' Day, keep All Saints' Day on November 1, and often choose a patron saint at baptism or confirmation.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Teresa of Kolkata, on the floor at Nirmal Hriday with the dying through years of darkness. Your line was small things with great love. Who did you really see? Today, the last day of the stories. Day ninety-six.

The last mile of a marathon. The legs are gone and the lungs are burning. Then the runner turns a corner, and both sides of the street are packed with people. Strangers, shouting the name printed on the bib. Some of them ran this race last year. Some ran it decades ago. They know this mile, and they're yelling: keep going, nearly there. An early Christian writer used a picture much like it in the Letter to the Hebrews. And it's the picture Catholics have in mind when they look at a church full of saints. Not statues. A crowd. Today's word is what binds that crowd together.
screen: `THE LAST MILE.` → `BOTH SIDES OF THE STREET, PACKED.` → `NOT STATUES. A CROWD.`

segments.voice: Hebrews chapter eleven is a roll call of people who kept faith: Abel, Noah, Abraham and Sarah, Moses, Rahab, and many more whose names the writer runs out of time to list. Then chapter twelve turns to the reader. In the Douay-Rheims: "having so great a cloud of witnesses over our head," let us lay down every weight and run the race. A cloud, not a handful. And the Greek word for witness is martys, which later gave us the word martyr. Witnesses who have finished, watching the ones still running. In the Apostles' Creed, said at baptisms and at the start of the rosary, Catholics say they believe in the communion of saints. It means the Church is one family across death. Catholics speak of it in three parts: those still on earth, those being made ready for God, and those already with God in heaven. Love goes across all three. That's why Catholics pray for the dead, and why they ask the saints to pray for them, the way you'd ask a friend. Think back over this camp. We started with two pregnant women meeting in the hill country, and a child with no room at the inn. Then fishermen, a woman at a well, a man through a roof, a lost son, a Samaritan on the road. A garden, a cross, an empty tomb, a road to Emmaus. Fire at Pentecost. Mary. And then the saints, one by one: Augustine, Patrick, Clare, Catherine, Joan, More, Bernadette, Thérèse, Kolbe, Teresa. Seventy-five days of stories. Catholics would say that's not a list of the dead. That's the crowd on the street.
screen: `A ROLL CALL IN HEBREWS ELEVEN.` · `A CLOUD OF WITNESSES, WATCHING.` · `ONE FAMILY ACROSS DEATH.` · `SEVENTY-FIVE DAYS OF STORIES.` · then, large: `SO GREAT A CLOUD OF WITNESSES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pick one saint to walk with this year. Settle, and breathe. Think back over the stories of this camp, and let one face come forward. Maybe the one who surprised you. Maybe the one who seems most like you, or least. Don't choose the most impressive one. Choose the one you'd want beside you on a bad day. Say their name once, quietly. If you pray, you can ask them to pray for you. The bell holds the time.
communio sanctorum. Latin for the communion of saints, the Church as one family across death, in prayer for each other.

Your line: so great a cloud of witnesses. That's Camp Two, the stories. Tomorrow Camp Three begins: the practices, starting at the church door. Today, when the mile gets long, remember the crowd. Day ninety-six.

97.title: First Mass, or first in years
97.hook: the hardest part is walking through the door; nobody at the door asks where you've been
97.howItsDone: Anyone may attend Mass. Visitors and returning Catholics sit where they like and follow the people around them; those not receiving Communion stay in the pew or, in many parishes, come forward with arms crossed for a blessing. Adults who wish to become Catholic join their parish's OCIA (formerly RCIA).

segments.voice: Yesterday, communio sanctorum, the communion of saints, and the close of the stories. Your line was so great a cloud of witnesses. Which saint did you pick to walk with? Now Camp Three: the practices. Day ninety-seven.

A church parking lot, ten minutes before Sunday Mass. Someone is sitting in a car with the engine off, watching families cross the lot. They haven't been inside in eleven years. Or they've never been inside at all, and a friend said, just come once. Their hands are a little sweaty. What if everyone can tell? What if I stand up at the wrong time? People who have made that walk say the same thing afterward: the hardest part was the door. Camp Two was the stories. Camp Three is the practices, what Catholics actually do. It starts there, in the parking lot. Today: the parish.
screen: `TEN MINUTES BEFORE MASS.` → `ELEVEN YEARS, OR NEVER.` → `THE HARDEST PART IS THE DOOR.`

segments.voice: First, the word. Parish comes from a Greek word, paroikia, for people living away from home: neighbors who are also, in a sense, strangers. The first letter of Peter calls Christians, in the Douay-Rheims, "strangers and pilgrims." So a parish was never a club for people who already belong. It's a house full of people on the way. Second, why people come, and why they stayed away. Some walk in for a funeral or a wedding. Some after a hard year, or for a partner, or out of plain curiosity. And people step away for all kinds of reasons too. Some stopped believing. Some were hurt. Some drifted, or were never really taught. Nobody at the door asks which. You're not behind. Third, what actually happens. Sit anywhere; the back is fine. There's usually a book or a card in the pew with the words. Stand, sit and kneel when the people around you do. Nobody is grading. When Communion comes, Catholics who are ready go up to receive. Anyone who isn't, a guest, someone on the way to becoming Catholic, a Catholic who isn't ready yet, can stay in the pew, or in many parishes come up with arms crossed over the chest for a blessing. Both are completely normal. Fourth, the next step, whenever you want one. Someone coming back can talk to a priest, and go to confession when they're ready; that's a whole lesson later on. Adults who want to become Catholic go through a process many parishes now call OCIA, the Order of Christian Initiation of Adults; it used to be called RCIA. Some lifelong Catholics sit in on it as a refresher. And the line people hear over and over, from the pew next to them, is two words: welcome home.
screen: `PARISH: STRANGERS AND PILGRIMS.` · `MANY REASONS TO LEAVE, AND TO COME.` · `SIT, STAND, KNEEL WITH EVERYONE.` · `ARMS CROSSED FOR A BLESSING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: walk in, in your mind. Settle, and breathe. Picture a church you know, or one you've driven past. See the doors. Feel your hand on the handle, and the small hush as it closes behind you. Find a seat near the back. Notice the light, the people, the quiet. Nobody turns around. Just sit there for a while, and let it be all right that you came. If you pray, you can say so, in a word or two. The bell holds the time.
Parish. From the Greek for people living away from home: the local church, a house of strangers and pilgrims, open to whoever walks in. Today's word.
Your line: welcome home. Whether it's your first Mass or your first in years, that's what the door is for. Tomorrow, the water just inside it. Day ninety-seven.

original.note: Greek: a sojourning, living as a neighbor away from home. Through Latin parochia it became parish.

trapdoor: what you thought: a parish is the church building, or the club of people who belong there.
what it means: the local community of Catholics, open to anyone who walks in, whether it's their first Mass or their first in years.

what a scholar hears: paroikia, from paroikos, a resident alien or sojourner. 1 Peter 2:11 calls Christians paroikous, "strangers and pilgrims"; the word for exiles became the word for the local church.

98.title: Holy water at the door
98.hook: touching water at the church door recalls your baptism
98.howItsDone: Catholics dip their fingers in holy water and make the sign of the cross on entering and often on leaving a church; many keep holy water at home, and at some Sunday Masses the priest sprinkles the congregation with it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the parish, and a first Mass, or a first in years. Your line was welcome home. Which door did you picture? Day ninety-eight.

A small basin of water, fixed to the wall or set on a pillar just inside a Catholic church door. People coming in stop at it before they've even looked up at the altar. They dip two fingers in, touch forehead, heart, shoulders, and walk on. Kids stretch on their toes to reach it. Some people flick a drop onto a friend. It takes two seconds, and a visitor could easily miss it. It's water. That's all. And it isn't all. Today: holy water at the door.
screen: `A BASIN BY THE DOOR.` → `TWO FINGERS, TWO SECONDS.` → `WATER, AND NOT ONLY WATER.`

segments.voice: The water in that basin has been blessed by a priest, with a prayer asking God to make it a sign of protection and a reminder of baptism. That second part is the key. For Catholics, the way into the Church is water. Often it was in infancy: a baby held over a font while a priest poured water three times and said the words from your very first day: in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. Jesus says in John's Gospel, in the Douay-Rheims: "unless a man be born again of water and the Holy Ghost, he cannot enter into the kingdom of God." Paul adds a picture. He says baptism is like being buried with Christ and rising with him. So when a Catholic walks into church and touches the water, the body is saying: I came in through water once. I'm coming in again. The door of the church echoes the door of baptism. Catholics call holy water a sacramental. That's a different thing from a sacrament. It isn't magic, and it doesn't work by itself. The Church teaches it's a blessed sign that prepares a person to receive grace, through the Church's prayer and the person's own faith. On some Sundays, especially in the Easter season, the priest walks down the aisle and sprinkles the whole congregation with it. Some people laugh when they get a good splash. Some families also keep a little holy water at home, by the front door or the bed. And this week's thread: a French girl digging for a spring, and now a basin at a door. Water keeps showing up.
screen: `BLESSED WATER, BY THE DOOR.` · `YOU CAME IN THROUGH WATER.` · `A SACRAMENTAL, NOT MAGIC.` · `SPRINKLED ON THE WHOLE CROWD.` · then, large: `BORN AGAIN OF WATER AND THE HOLY GHOST.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: the water at your tap. If you can, go to a sink, or picture one. Let the water run over your fingers. It isn't holy water. It's a reminder, the way a photo reminds you of a face. If you're Catholic, or you'd like to, touch your forehead with the wet fingers, or make the sign of the cross. If not, just feel the cold, and remember one beginning in your own life. Then sit. The bell holds the time.
aqua benedicta. Latin for blessed water, touched at the church door to remember the water of baptism.

Your line: every door a baptism. This week ran from Lourdes, through Thérèse, Kolbe and Teresa, to the cloud of witnesses, and into the practices. Today, at one doorway, pause for a second, and walk through it like a new start. Day ninety-eight.

original.note: Latin: blessed water, the Church's old name for holy water.

what it means: blessed water that Catholics touch on the way in, remembering the water they were baptized in.
what a scholar hears: a sacramental, not a sacrament. it prepares for grace through the Church's prayer, and the sprinkling rite at Mass once opened with a psalm verse.
